Borrowed from French révision, from Latin revīsiō.
Borrowed from French récitatif, from Italian recitativo.

parole.significato: rhesus monkey, rhesus macaque, Macaca mulatta
parole.testo: From French rhésus + Affe (“ape, monkey”), partial calque of French singe rhésus.

parole.significato: rival (opponent striving for the same goal, e.g. in competition or courtship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rival, initially as Rival (which Grimm still lists as the only form). In the 19th century, the singular was suffixed with -e, which Pfeifer suggests may have been a reanalysis a previously strong plural..

parole.significato: a long, formal dress worn only on special occasions
castling (move consisting of the castle (rook) and king swapping places)
parole.testo: 19th century, from rochieren + -ade, after French rocade.

parole.significato: to castle (perform the move of castling)

Alteration (based on rollen, Rollladen) of older Rouleau, from French rouleau.
Ca. 1898, from rollen (“to roll”) + Treppe (“staircase”), possibly after French escalier roulant (of roughly contemporaneous attestation).
Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from English rummy + French -é.

parole.significato: rosette, a shape like that of a rose

parole.testo: From French royal, from Latin regalis. Occasionally attested in the 19th century and perhaps earlier. Borrowed from French rudimentaire, from French rudiment, from Latin rudimentum.

parole.significato: ruin (something which leads to serious troubles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ruine, from Latin ruīna. Doublet of Ruine.

parole.significato: to ruin (to destroy or make dysfunctional, e.g. of health, relationships or financially)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ruiner. Equivalent to Ruine or Ruin + -ieren.

Uncertain. Possibly from French rondiste or Italian rondista.

Ca. 1900, unadapted borrowing from French sabotage. By surface analysis, sabotieren + -age.
From Middle High German safrān; derived from French safran, from Arabic زعفران (zāfarān). Cognate with English saffron, Spanish azafrán, Italian zafferano.

parole.significato: to seize, to divest of possession by act of public authority
season (a part of a year when something particular happens)

parole.testo: From Saison + -al. A pseudo-Gallicism, perhaps modeled on English seasonal (compare French saisonnier).

parole.significato: saccade (rapid jerky movement of the eye (voluntary or involuntary) from one focus to another)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French saccade, probably from Spanish sacar (“to take out”), perhaps from Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌺𐌰𐌽 (sakan, “dispute, rebuke”).

parole.significato: very casual, informal, possibly to the degree of being sloppy, rakish, flippant
parole.testo: 18th century, from French salope, adjectival use of salope (“slovenly woman”). Compare German schlampig.
Borrowed from French salut, from Latin salus.

parole.significato: salvo (simultaneous discharge of artillery or firearms including the firing of guns either to hit a target or to perfor…

parole.testo: Borrowed from French salut (“hello”, greeting), from Latin salūs (“health”).

parole.significato: a type of elegant (often high-heeled) sandal

parole.testo: Borrowed from French saperlotte (17th century), euphemistic modification of sacredieu, from sacré (nom de) Dieu (literally “holy (name of) God”).

Borrowed from French sarcophage, from Latin sarcophagus, from Ancient Greek σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos, “coffin of limestone”, noun), from σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos, “flesh-eating, carnivorous”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh, meat”) + -φάγος (-phágos).
Borrowed from French satin, from Arabic زَيْتُون (zaytūn, “Zayton; olive”).
Borrowed from French sauce, from Old French sauce, sause, sausse, salse, from Latin salsa.

From French savanne, from Spanish sabana, from Taíno.
19th century, from French saxophone. Equivalent to the name Adolphe Sax + -o- + -fon, from Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice”).

From French chic, itself from German Schick (“correct manners, correct clothing”).

Possibly from French je m'en fous.
Calque of French neiges d'antan (“yesteryear's snow”), in German literally, “yesterday's snow”. Compare English where are the snows of yesteryear.

Borrowed from French choquer. Doublet of schocken.

parole.significato: liquid measure, historically and regionally varying, usually 0.4 to 0.5 liters

parole.significato: aesthete, belletrist (someone who cultivates a high sensitivity to beauty, particularly in the arts)
parole.testo: Calque of French bel esprit, schön + Geist.

parole.significato: a person who drives his or her own vehicle, rather than being driven by a chauffeur

Borrowed from French céleri, from Lombard selleri, from Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon). Introduced in the 17th century as a culinary term; celery was unusual in German cuisine before that time.

parole.significato: semantics (study of the meaning of words)

parole.testo: From French sentimentalité, with assimilation to nativized suffix -ität.

parole.significato: private room (room accessible only to those who have reserved it)

17th century, from French sérail, from Italian serraglio, from Ottoman Turkish سرای (seray, saray), from Persian سرای (sarây).
Borrowed from French sérénade, from Italian serenata.

parole.significato: reputable, respectable, dignified; not shady or dubious; appearing civil, reliable, legitimate

parole.significato: siglum, a conventional abbreviation for a word or words
parole.testo: From French sigle, from Latin sigillum. Doublet of Siegel.

parole.significato: to simplify (to portray something as less complex than it actually is, either to instruct or to mislead)
trap (bend in a pipe that prevents the escape of gases)

parole.significato: overcautious, scrupulous (anxiously concerned with avoiding mistakes; full of scruples and reservations)

Borrowed from French socle, from Italian zoccolo (“wooden shoe”), from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock”).

parole.significato: sofa, couch (upholstered seat with a raised back that accommodates at least two people)
parole.testo: 17th century, from French sofa, from Italian sofà, from Ottoman Turkish صفه (sofa), from Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa).

Originally the past participle of rare soignieren (“to maintain (one's style), to appear serious”), from French soigner (“to care for”), probably from Frankish *sunnjōn (“to deal with”). Compare French soigné.

From French solitaire (“solitary”), from Latin sōlitārius.

parole.significato: probe (device used to explore, investigate or measure)

parole.significato: sovereign (holder of the most fundamental authority in a political system)

parole.significato: Alpine valerian, valerian spikenard (the Alpine plant Valeriana celtica used in perfumery)

Borrowed from French sportif, equivalent to Sport + -iv.

parole.significato: internship, job that a trainee is doing in a workplace until a fixed date

parole.significato: stereotype (a conventional, formulaic, and oversimplified conception, opinion, or image)

parole.significato: suite (hotel apartment consisting of several rooms)

parole.significato: agenda; order of the day (business to be done by a body or group of people on a particular day)
parole.testo: 18th century, from Tag (“day”) + -es- + Ordnung (“order”), a calque of French ordre du jour, itself apparently a calque of English order of the day.

parole.significato: tactics, strategy (art of anticipation and planning)
parole.testo: 18th century, from French tactique, from Ancient Greek τακτική (τέχνη) (taktikḗ (tékhnē)).

parole.significato: talmi, an alloy of mostly zinc and copper and occasionally some tin and lead and about a percent of gold used for jewel…

parole.significato: royalty, tantième (performance-related compensation to an artist, employee or manager)
tapir (large odd-toed ungulate with long prehensile upper lip)

Borrowed from French télégraphier. Equivalent to Telegraph + -ieren.

parole.significato: temporary (for a limited time, ephemeral, not constant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French temporaire, from Latin temporārius, from tempus (“time”).
Relatinized from French tendance under the influence of Medieval Latin tendentia.

parole.significato: terrace (raised, flat-topped bank of earth with sloping sides)

parole.testo: From French tertiaire, from Medieval Latin tertiarius.

parole.significato: theater (a place or building consisting of a stage and seats)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French théâtre, utimately from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see, watch, observe”).
Borrowed from French tomate or Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl (“tomatillo”), the tomato proper being xītomatl.
Borrowed from French tour de force.
By surface analysis, Tradition + -ell. Borrowed from French traditionnel.

parole.significato: to carve, to slice (meat or other foods)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French translation, from Latin trānslātiō.

staircase wit; l'esprit de l'escalier; a remark or rejoinder thought of only when it is too late
parole.testo: From Treppe (“stairs, steps”) + -n- + Witz (“wit”), a calque of French esprit de l'escalier.

Borrowed from French tribune, from Italian tribuna.

parole.significato: treble (the winning of three competitions in one year, usually national league and cup plus an international title)

parole.significato: uniform (distinctive outfit as a means of identifying members of a group)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French uniforme, from Latin uniformis.

From un- + Stern, calque of French désastre.

parole.significato: Ursuline (member of the Order of Saint Ursula)

parole.significato: verlan (type of backslang used in French)

parole.significato: a Swiss dessert made from sweet chestnut paste formed into worm-like strands, and topped with whipped cream or ice cream
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vermicelles f pl (“vermicelli”, literally “little worms”).

parole.significato: vernissage (private, invite-only exhibition of an artist's work)

17th century, borrowed from French visage (“face”). Early on often pejoratively, to which context it was ultimately restricted.

parole.significato: waistcoat, vest (usually sleeveless garment worn over a shirt)
parole.testo: 17th century, from French veste. At first also Veste, though the spelling with W- has always been predominant; perhaps to distinguish it from Veste (“fortress”).
